svg.aria-label: The elongation stage and the fidelity of transcription: the polymerase unwinding ahead and rewinding behind with its RNA-DNA hybrid, several polymerases queued along one gene, the supercoils transcription creates and the role of topoisomerase, and the logic that the difference in error rate between replication and transcription follows from the reversibility of the outcome.
svg.text: A Several polymerases on one gene, and the supercoils they make
once the first polymerase has moved far enough the promoter is free and the next can initiate
in an active gene they run in a queue, which looks like a feather in the electron microscope
positive supercoil ahead
negative supercoil behind
topoisomerase
without it transcription stalls
B Speed is not constant
50 to 100 nt/s in bacteria, 20 to 80 nt/s in humans — but the
polymerase slows or stops at particular sequences.
Pol II pausing is one case; termination begins with a stop.
Elongation speed also influences splice-site choice: slower passage gives a weak site time to be used.
C Fidelity, and why it is lower
replication
10^-9 to 10^-10, proofreading exonuclease
transcription
10^-4 to 10^-5, almost no proofreading
a difference of more than ten thousandfold
A replication error is permanent and passes to every descendant.
A transcription error sits in ONE RNA, which is soon degraded —
and thousands of mRNA are made from one gene.
Accuracy is matched to whether the error can be undone.
Permanent outcomes get layered proofreading; temporary ones do not. Translation (about 10^-4) follows the same rule.
